shortTitle: Choosing a model for a table
title: Choosing a model for a table
hook: Simple, tree-based, ensembles, neighbors, or a neural network. What table data usually wants.
inPlainWords: You do not need the hardest model. You need the right one. For rows and columns, start simple, then try tree-based ensembles.

useCase.title: Predict which of 20,000 customers will cancel
useCase.story: Columns: months as a customer, orders, support tickets, average basket, days since last visit. The answer is known for past customers: cancelled or stayed. Managers also want to know the reasons.

approaches.name: Simple linear model (logistic regression)
approaches.what: Adds up weighted clues into a score.
approaches.greatWhen: You want a baseline, clear explanations, or you have small data.
approaches.example: Each extra support ticket raises the cancel risk a little.

approaches.name: Decision tree
approaches.what: A flowchart of yes or no questions learned from data.
approaches.greatWhen: You must show the rules to non-technical people.
approaches.avoidWhen: On its own it memorizes the data.
approaches.example: Many tickets and no visit for 60 days means likely to cancel.

approaches.name: Random forest
approaches.what: Many trees vote on the answer.
approaches.greatWhen: You want strong results with few settings to tune.
approaches.avoidWhen: You need a tiny, very fast model.
approaches.example: 200 trees vote on whether a customer cancels.

approaches.name: Gradient boosting
approaches.what: Trees built one after another, each one fixing the last one's mistakes.
approaches.greatWhen: You want the best accuracy on a table. It is often the winner.
approaches.avoidWhen: You will not spend time tuning it, or you cannot guard against overfitting.
approaches.example: The usual top performer for cancellation risk.

approaches.name: Nearest neighbors
approaches.what: Find the most similar past customers and copy their outcome.
approaches.greatWhen: Data is small and similarity is meaningful.
approaches.avoidWhen: Data is large or has many columns. It is slow and touchy.
approaches.example: Customers like this one mostly stayed.

approaches.name: Neural network
approaches.avoidWhen: Small tables. It is usually no better, and harder to explain.

challenge.question: You need good accuracy and a way to explain the main reasons to managers. What is the smart path?

options.text: Start with a simple baseline, then try boosted trees, and explain the top reasons per customer
options.why: The baseline tells you what "good" means, boosted trees usually win on tables, and the reasons keep managers on board.

options.text: Go straight to a neural network
options.why: No baseline to compare, more effort, and harder to explain.
Easy to read, but it tends to memorize the data.
Slow on this size, and it gives no clear reasons.

bestCase.title: Baseline first, then boosted trees, explained with top reasons
bestCase.example: A simple model gets a fair score and clear reasons. Boosted trees beat it. Managers see the top three reasons for each flagged customer: many tickets, a long gap since the last visit, and a shrinking basket.

worstCase.title: The fanciest model first, with no baseline
worstCase.example: A deep network scores 91% and nobody knows if that is good, because a simple model would have scored 90%. It is slower, costlier, and cannot explain why a loyal customer was flagged.

route.travelling: Customer 3021: 14 months, 3 tickets, no visit for 70 days

steps.label: Customer table
steps.goes: 20,000 customers, each marked cancelled or stayed.

steps.label: Simple baseline
steps.goes: A quick model is 84% right. That is the number to beat.

steps.label: Try stronger models
steps.goesWrong: The team skips the baseline and trains a deep network. There is nothing to compare it with.

steps.label: Compare on the exam set
steps.goes: Pick the best on data none of the models saw.

steps.label: Explain the top reasons
steps.goes: Three tickets and 70 days away drive this customer's risk.

steps.label: Serve and watch
steps.goes: Risk scores go to the retention team every week.

takeaway: Beat a simple baseline before reaching for anything fancy. On tables, tree-based ensembles usually win.
